headline: Massachusetts offers businesses up to $25,000 to explore employee ownership
dek: A new state program will cover half the eligible cost of feasibility studies, valuations, legal work and transaction planning for companies considering ESOPs or worker cooperatives.
body: Massachusetts is offering financial help to businesses that want to determine whether employee ownership could provide a path for succession, job retention or long-term growth. The Healey-Driscoll administration announced Tuesday that the Massachusetts Center for Employee Ownership, or MassCEO, has launched a technical-assistance stipend program that will cover 50% of eligible pre-conversion costs. The [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-launches-new-program-to-help-businesses-explore-employee-ownership) says companies can receive as much as $25,000 for an Employee Stock Ownership Plan project or $12,500 for a worker-cooperative project.

The money is intended for the work that comes before a sale or conversion. Eligible expenses include feasibility studies, business valuations, legal services and transaction planning. MassCEO will connect applicants with qualified consultants it selects, while businesses apply on a rolling basis subject to available funding. That structure matters: the new program helps an owner investigate whether a transition is workable, but it does not announce that the state will finance the purchase of a company or guarantee that an application will be approved.

The two main models named by the state give workers different forms of ownership. In an ESOP, a trust generally holds company stock for employees through a retirement-plan structure. In a worker cooperative, employees become members and use a democratic governance model to make decisions about the business. The [MassCEO program page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-center-for-employee-ownership) describes both as options alongside employee-ownership trusts, another structure in which employees are the intended beneficiaries of a continuing trust. The choice affects financing, governance, taxes, retirement benefits and how much decision-making authority workers receive, so the stipend is aimed at professional analysis rather than a one-size-fits-all conversion.

Massachusetts has been building a public infrastructure around that analysis. The U.S. Department of Labor’s [Employee Ownership Initiative overview](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/about-ebsa/our-activities/programs-and-initiatives/employee-ownership-initiative/tools-and-resources/employee-ownership-states) identifies the Massachusetts Center for Employee Ownership as an office created through the state’s 2022 economic-development legislation and notes that the center has a 19-member advisory board. A [2025 annual report filed with the Massachusetts Legislature](https://malegislature.gov/Reports/29314/%28144%29%20CY25%20MassCEO%20Annual%20Report.pdf) says the center’s statutory mission includes education, outreach, research, grants and efforts to increase the number of employee-owned companies. The new stipend puts one part of that mission into a direct service for business owners.

For a closely held Massachusetts company, the issue is often less about a corporate label than about what happens when an owner wants to retire, sell or step away. A conventional sale can move a company’s headquarters, jobs or decision-making outside the community. An employee-ownership study can test whether the existing workforce, management team and finances could support another route. That possibility is a policy goal, not a reported outcome of this program: the state has not announced how many companies will convert or how many jobs the stipends will preserve.

The program also leaves important questions for applicants. The state announcement does not set out a single application deadline, a statewide award target or a total program budget; it directs businesses to MassCEO’s information page and says assistance depends on available funding. Owners will need to confirm eligibility, the list of approved providers and which costs qualify before committing to a study. A business that receives help to explore an ESOP or cooperative can still decide that the structure is not financially or operationally suitable.

That review phase is the immediate news for Massachusetts businesses. The state is lowering the price of specialized advice at the point when an owner is deciding whether employee ownership is realistic, while leaving the ultimate decision with the company and its workers. Applications and program details are available through [MassCEO](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-center-for-employee-ownership); the center’s contact information lists Kevin Kuros as director and identifies the Massachusetts Office of Business Development as its home. Any later conversion, financing agreement or change in company ownership would be a separate development that should be reported on its own terms.
